statement: Let $x_1, x_2$ be complex numbers and $y_1, y_2, y_3$ complex numbers, each family [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then at least one of the six numbers $e^{x_i y_j}$ is a [transcendental number](c:transcendental-number).

hypotheses.text: The numbers $x_1, x_2$ are [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) over $\mathbb{Q}$.
The numbers $y_1, y_2, y_3$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: At least one of the numbers $e^{x_i y_j}$, with $i \in \{1,2\}$ and $j \in \{1,2,3\}$, is [transcendental](c:transcendental-number).

proofs.name: Schneider's method with an auxiliary function
proofs.slogan: Assume all six numbers are algebraic, build an auxiliary function with many zeros, extend its zeros to a lattice and contradict independence.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, as an outline: Siegel's lemma, the Schwarz lemma and Liouville's inequality are taken from the cited work. The same proof gives the version with $d$ numbers $x_i$ and $\ell$ numbers $y_j$ when $d\ell > d + \ell$.

roles.why: Independence of $x_1, x_2$ makes the exponents $ax_1+bx_2$ distinct, so $F$ is not the zero function.
Independence of the $y_j$ makes the points $s_1y_1+s_2y_2+s_3y_3$ distinct, and $2 \cdot 3 > 2 + 3$ makes the count work.

steps.slogan: Assume that the six numbers $e^{x_iy_j}$ are all [algebraic](c:algebraic-number) and lie in one [number field](c:number-field) $K$.
steps.detail: Every number $e^{(ax_1+bx_2)(s_1y_1+s_2y_2+s_3y_3)}$ with integers $a,b,s_j \ge 0$ is a product of powers of the six numbers. So it lies in $K$, and its size and denominator are controlled by $a,b,s_j$.

steps.slogan: Construct a nonzero function $F(z)=\sum c_{ab}e^{(ax_1+bx_2)z}$ that vanishes at many lattice points.
steps.detail: Take $0 \le a,b < L$ and integer coefficients $c_{ab}$. Vanishing of $F$ at the $N^3$ points $s_1y_1+s_2y_2+s_3y_3$ with $0 \le s_j < N$ is a linear system over $K$. For $L^2$ large against $N^3$, Siegel's lemma gives a nonzero integer solution of controlled size, and $F \ne 0$ because the exponents are distinct.

steps.slogan: Extend the zeros of $F$ from the box of size $N$ to every lattice point.
steps.detail: At a lattice point just outside the box, the Schwarz lemma bounds $|F|$ by a very small number. If $F$ were nonzero there, it would be a nonzero element of $K$, and Liouville's inequality gives a larger lower bound. So $F$ vanishes there, and by induction on the box size at all $s\cdot y$ with $s \in \mathbb{N}^3$.

steps.slogan: Show that vanishing at all lattice points forces every coefficient $c_{ab}$ to be zero.
steps.detail: Put $\xi_{abj}=e^{(ax_1+bx_2)y_j}$, so $F(s\cdot y)=\sum c_{ab}\xi_{ab1}^{s_1}\xi_{ab2}^{s_2}\xi_{ab3}^{s_3}$. The triples $(\xi_{abj})_j$ differ for different $(a,b)$: equality gives $\lambda y_j \in 2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$ for all $j$ with $\lambda\ne0$, which makes the $y_j$ rational multiples of one number. Distinct characters of $\mathbb{N}^3$ are linearly independent, so all $c_{ab}=0$.

steps.slogan: Reach a contradiction and conclude that some $e^{x_iy_j}$ is [transcendental](c:transcendental-number).
steps.detail: Step 2 gives integers $c_{ab}$ that are not all zero, and step 4 gives $c_{ab}=0$ for all $a,b$. So the assumption of step 1 is false.

concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence of the $x_i$ and of the $y_j$ makes exponents and points distinct.
concepts.c:transcendental-number: The theorem says that one of the six exponentials is transcendental.
concepts.c:algebraic-number: The contradiction hypothesis makes all six exponentials algebraic numbers.
concepts.c:number-field: One number field $K$ holds every value of the auxiliary function.

source.ref: S. Lang, Introduction to Transcendental Numbers, Addison-Wesley, Reading, Massachusetts, 1966 (the theorem is due to Siegel, Lang and Ramachandra)
source.note: Lang's auxiliary function proof in Schneider's method; the outline uses d = 2 exponents and l = 3 points.

statement: Fix a prime $p$ and an integer $n \ge 0$, and let $L_n$ be [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) at the [Johnson-Wilson theory](c:johnson-wilson-theory) $E(n)$. Then for every spectrum $X$ the natural map $X \wedge L_nS \to L_nX$ is an equivalence. In other words, $L_n$ is a [smashing localization](c:smashing-localization).

hypotheses.text: The prime $p$ and the integer $n \ge 0$ are fixed, and spectra are $p$-local.
The object $X$ is a spectrum.

conclusion: The natural map $X \wedge L_nS \to L_nX$ is an equivalence for every spectrum $X$.

proofs.name: Nilpotence and a vanishing line
proofs.slogan: Show that $L_nS$ is $E(n)$-nilpotent by a uniform vanishing line in its Adams-Novikov spectral sequence, which makes $L_n$ smashing.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, as an outline: the algebraic computations and the control of differentials rest on the cited work. The telescope conjecture ($L_n$ equals the finite localization) is a different statement, and it fails for $n \ge 2$.

roles.why: Each prime and each height has its own $E(n)$, and the proof treats them one at a time.
The final equivalence is natural in $X$; a spectrum is smashed with $L_nS$.

steps.slogan: Reduce smashing to a nilpotence property of the sphere $L_nS$.
steps.detail: A localization is smashing exactly when $X \wedge L_nS$ is already $E(n)$-local for every $X$. This holds when $L_nS$ is $E(n)$-nilpotent, that is, built from finitely many $E(n)$-modules, because $E(n)$-modules are $E(n)$-local.

steps.slogan: Turn nilpotence into a statement about the $E(n)$-based Adams tower of $L_nS$.
steps.detail: Standard nilpotence technology, which rests on the nilpotence theorem, shows that $L_nS$ is $E(n)$-nilpotent if its Adams tower is pro-constant. The tower is the cobar tower of the [Adams-Novikov spectral sequence](c:adams-novikov-spectral-sequence) for $L_nS$.

steps.slogan: Find a horizontal vanishing line, at a finite page, in the spectral sequence of $L_nS$.
steps.detail: Morava's change of rings expresses the $E_2$-term through the cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group acting on [Morava E-theory](c:morava-e-theory). That cohomology vanishes high up when $p-1 \nmid n$. Hopkins and Ravenel obtain a vanishing line at a finite page at every prime and every $n$.

steps.slogan: Convert the vanishing line into a uniform bound on the length of the tower.
steps.detail: A vanishing line at a finite page bounds the filtration in which nonzero classes survive. So the maps from stage $N$ of the tower to the first stage are null for one fixed $N$, and the tower is pro-constant.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $L_nS$ is $E(n)$-nilpotent, so $X \wedge L_nS \to L_nX$ is an equivalence.
steps.detail: A pro-constant tower exhibits $L_nS$ as a retract of one finite stage, which is built from finitely many $E(n)$-modules. So $L_nS$ is $E(n)$-nilpotent. By step 1, $X \wedge L_nS$ is $E(n)$-local, and the natural map to $L_nX$ is an equivalence.

concepts.c:bousfield-localization: The theorem is about Bousfield localization at $E(n)$.
concepts.c:johnson-wilson-theory: $E(n)$ is the homology theory whose acyclics define $L_n$.
concepts.c:smashing-localization: Smashing is the property that $L_nX$ equals $X \wedge L_nS$.
concepts.c:adams-novikov-spectral-sequence: Its vanishing line controls the length of the Adams tower.
concepts.c:morava-e-theory: Its stabilizer-group cohomology gives the $E_2$-term of the spectral sequence.

source.ref: D. C. Ravenel, Nilpotence and Periodicity in Stable Homotopy Theory, Annals of Mathematics Studies 128, Princeton University Press, 1992 (Theorem 7.5.6, proved in Chapter 8; after M. J. Hopkins and D. C. Ravenel)
source.note: The outline follows the reformulation of the theorem as pro-constancy of the E(n)-Adams tower of L_nS, proved through a uniform vanishing line.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $X$ a connected finite-dimensional [CW complex](c:cw-complex). Then the space $\mathrm{Map}_*(BG, X)$ of pointed maps from the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$ is weakly [contractible](c:contractible-space). Equivalently, the constant maps $X \to \mathrm{Map}(BG, X)$ form a weak equivalence.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
The space $X$ is a connected finite-dimensional [CW complex](c:cw-complex).

conclusion: Every homotopy group of $\mathrm{Map}_*(BG, X)$ vanishes, so the space is weakly [contractible](c:contractible-space).

proofs.name: Miller's theorem
proofs.slogan: Reduce to cyclic groups of prime order, then use Carlsson's unstable module and a mod $p$ cohomology computation to kill the mapping space.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, as an outline of Miller's proof; the cohomology computation rests on the cited paper. The paper covers locally finite groups, and the fixed-point form ($X^G \to X^{hG}$ after $p$-completion for a finite $p$-group, with [homotopy fixed points](c:homotopy-fixed-point)) follows from it.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ lets the proof reduce to cyclic groups of prime order and to $p$-torsion homology.
Finite dimension makes the mod $p$ cohomology of $X$ vanish above a fixed degree, which drives the computation.

steps.slogan: Reduce the finite group $G$ to cyclic groups $\mathbb{Z}/p$ of prime order.
steps.detail: The cited paper shows that contractibility of $\mathrm{Map}_*(B\mathbb{Z}/p, K)$ for every finite-dimensional $K$ and every prime $p$ gives the theorem for all finite and locally finite groups $G$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the [p-adic completion](c:p-adic-completion) of the target, where cohomology detects equivalences.
steps.detail: The space $B\mathbb{Z}/p$ is connected and has only $p$-torsion homology. So pointed maps from it see only the $p$-completion of the target, and a mod $p$ cohomology computation can decide contractibility.

steps.slogan: Use Carlsson's description of the homology of $B\mathbb{Z}/p$ as a module over the [Steenrod algebra](c:steenrod-algebra).
steps.detail: Carlsson computes $H_*(B\mathbb{Z}/2)$ as an unstable module over the Steenrod algebra. This computation is the algebraic input that Miller's calculation needs, and Lannes's T-functor later gave a second route.

steps.slogan: Compute the mod $p$ cohomology of $\mathrm{Map}_*(B\mathbb{Z}/p, X)$ for finite-dimensional $X$ and find it trivial.
steps.detail: Miller builds the cohomology of the mapping space from the cohomology of $X$ and the unstable module of step 3 with spectral sequences. Because $H^*(X;\mathbb{F}_p)$ vanishes above the dimension of $X$, the algebraic terms vanish, and the reduced cohomology of the mapping space is zero.

steps.slogan: Convert vanishing cohomology into weak contractibility and assemble all primes.
steps.detail: The mod $p$ Whitehead theorem turns zero reduced mod $p$ cohomology into contractibility after $p$-completion. Rational and other-prime parts vanish because $BG$ has only torsion homology, so $\mathrm{Map}_*(BG,X)$ is weakly contractible.

concepts.c:cw-complex: Finite dimension of the CW complex is the hypothesis that the proof uses.
concepts.c:classifying-space: The source $BG$ of the pointed maps is the classifying space.
concepts.c:contractible-space: The theorem says that the mapping space is weakly contractible.
concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness of $G$ gives torsion homology and the reduction to $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
concepts.c:homotopy-fixed-point: The fixed-point form of the conjecture compares fixed points with homotopy fixed points.
concepts.c:p-adic-completion: Completion at $p$ lets mod $p$ cohomology decide contractibility.
concepts.c:steenrod-algebra: Its unstable modules encode the cohomology of $B\mathbb{Z}/p$ and of $X$.

source.ref: H. Miller, The Sullivan conjecture on maps from classifying spaces, Annals of Mathematics 120 (1984), 39-87
source.note: Miller's Theorem A covers locally finite groups; the outline follows its reduction to Z/p, Carlsson's input and the cohomology computation.

statement: The reciprocals of the [triangular numbers](c:triangular-number) $T_n = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n = n(n+1)/2$ have sum $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 1/T_n = 2$.
conclusion: The [series](c:series) $\sum_{n \ge 1} 2/(n(n+1))$ converges and its sum is $2$.

proofs.name: Telescoping partial sums
proofs.slogan: Split each term into two unit fractions so that the partial sums telescope to $2 - 2/(N+1)$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for $n \ge 1$. No hypothesis is needed beyond the definition of $T_n$.

steps.slogan: Write the reciprocal of the [triangular number](c:triangular-number) $T_n$ as $2/(n(n+1))$.
steps.detail: Pair the terms $k$ and $n+1-k$ of $1+2+\cdots+n$. Each pair has sum $n+1$ and there are $n/2$ pairs, so $T_n = n(n+1)/2$ and $1/T_n = 2/(n(n+1))$.

steps.slogan: Split each term into a difference of two unit fractions.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 1$ we have $\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1}$. So $\frac{1}{T_n} = 2\left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1}\right)$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the inner terms of the [partial sum](c:partial-sum) $S_N$.
steps.detail: We get $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} 1/T_n = 2\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right) + 2\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) + \cdots$, and every middle term cancels. So $S_N = 2 - \frac{2}{N+1}$.

steps.slogan: Let $N$ grow and read the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of the partial sums.
steps.detail: The sequence $S_N = 2 - 2/(N+1)$ increases and tends to $2$. So the series converges and its sum is $2$.

concepts.c:triangular-number: The terms of the series are reciprocals of triangular numbers.
concepts.c:series: The theorem gives the sum of a series.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The partial sums have a closed form that shows the limit.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The sum of the series is the limit of its partial sums.

source.note: The classical telescoping sum, found by Leibniz after a question of Huygens.

statement: Let $k$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $K$ a finitely generated field extension of $k$ of transcendence degree $1$ (the [function field](c:function-field-of-a-variety) of a curve). Then $K$ is [quasi-algebraically closed](c:quasi-algebraically-closed-field): every [homogeneous polynomial](c:homogeneous-polynomial) of degree $d$ in $n > d$ variables over $K$ has a nontrivial zero in $K^n$.

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ is an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The field $K$ is finitely generated over $k$ and has transcendence degree $1$.

conclusion: Every form of degree $d$ in $n > d$ variables over $K$ has a nontrivial zero in $K^n$.

proofs.name: Counting unknowns and equations
proofs.slogan: Solve the form over $k(t)$ by counting unknowns and equations, then pass to a finite extension through its norm form.
proofs.scope: The full $C_1$ property of $K$. The vanishing of the [Brauer group](c:brauer-group) of $K$ and of the groups $H^i(K,K^*)$ are other members of the family and are not proved here.

roles.why: Algebraic closedness of $k$ gives a common nontrivial zero of $r$ forms in more than $r$ unknowns.
Transcendence degree $1$ makes $K$ a finite extension of $k(t)$, so the norm form reduces $K$ to $k(t)$.

steps.slogan: Write $K$ as a finite extension of the rational function field $k(t)$.
steps.detail: Since $K$ has transcendence degree $1$, some $t \in K$ is transcendental over $k$. The field $K$ is finitely generated and algebraic over $k(t)$, so $[K:k(t)] = m < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the problem to $k(t)$ using the norm form of $K$ over $k(t)$.
steps.detail: Let $w_1,\dots,w_m$ be a basis of $K$ over $k(t)$ and $f$ a [form](c:homogeneous-polynomial) of degree $d<n$ over $K$. Write $x_i=\sum_j x_{ij}w_j$ with $x_{ij} \in k(t)$. Then $N_{K/k(t)}(f(x))$ is a form of degree $dm$ in $nm>dm$ variables over $k(t)$, and a nontrivial zero of it gives $x\neq0$ with $f(x)=0$.

steps.slogan: Substitute polynomials of bounded degree in $t$ for the variables of a form over $k(t)$.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be a form of degree $d<n$ over $k(t)$. Clear denominators so that its coefficients are polynomials in $t$ of degree at most $e$. Put $x_i=\sum_{j=0}^{s} a_{ij}t^j$ with unknowns $a_{ij} \in k$.

steps.slogan: Count the equations that $f(x)=0$ gives for the coefficients of $t$.
steps.detail: The polynomial $f(x)$ has degree at most $ds+e$ in $t$. So $f(x)=0$ is a system of $ds+e+1$ homogeneous equations of degree $d$ in the $n(s+1)$ unknowns $a_{ij}$. Because $n>d$, we have $n(s+1) > ds+e+1$ for $s$ large.

steps.slogan: Solve the system over $k$ and transfer the zero back to $K$.
steps.detail: Over an algebraically closed field, $r$ homogeneous equations in more than $r$ unknowns have a common nontrivial zero. So some $a_{ij}$ are not all zero, and the polynomials $x_i(t)$ give a nontrivial zero of $f$ over $k(t)$. Step 2 then gives a nontrivial zero over $K$.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: The unknowns $a_{ij}$ live in an algebraically closed field.
concepts.c:function-field-of-a-variety: The field $K$ is the function field of a curve.
concepts.c:quasi-algebraically-closed-field: The theorem says that $K$ is quasi-algebraically closed ($C_1$).
concepts.c:homogeneous-polynomial: Homogeneity makes the norm of the form a form again, so the count applies.
concepts.c:brauer-group: The Brauer group of $K$ vanishes as a consequence of the theorem.

source.note: Tsen's counting argument for k(t) and Lang's norm-form passage to finite extensions (see Serre, Galois Cohomology, II.3).

statement: Let $X$ be a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface), $f$ a nonconstant [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on $X$ of degree $d$, and $\omega$ a holomorphic $1$-form. Let $P_1(t),\dots,P_d(t)$ be the points of $f^{-1}(t)$. Then $\Phi(t)=\sum_i \int_{Q_i}^{P_i(t)}\omega$ is constant while $t$ moves, with paths continued along the motion of $t$.

hypotheses.text: The surface $X$ is a compact connected Riemann surface, that is, a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve).
The function $f$ is meromorphic and nonconstant, of degree $d$.
The form $\omega$ is holomorphic on $X$, so $\int \omega$ is an [abelian integral](c:abelian-integral) of the first kind.

conclusion: The sum $\Phi(t)$ of the integrals of $\omega$ to the points of the moving fibre is constant; other choices of paths change it by periods of $\omega$.

proofs.name: Trace of the form
proofs.slogan: Sum the form over the sheets of $f$, show that this trace is a holomorphic form on the sphere, and conclude that it is zero.
proofs.scope: The first-kind case of the theorem, with the moving curve given by the fibres of $f$. Differentials of the second and third kinds give rational functions and logarithms instead of a constant, and the Abel-Jacobi form for principal divisors is another member of the family.

roles.why: Compactness makes $f$ a finite covering away from finitely many branch values.
The degree $d$ gives $d$ local sheets, and the branch values are finite in number.
A holomorphic form has a power series in each local coordinate, which makes the trace holomorphic at branch points.

steps.slogan: Define the trace $\tau=\sum_i g_i^*\omega$ over the local inverse branches $g_i$ of $f$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be the finite set of branch values of $f$. Over $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus B$ the map $f$ is a $d$-sheeted covering, with holomorphic local inverses $g_1,\dots,g_d$. The sum $\tau=\sum_i g_i^*\omega$ does not depend on the order of the sheets, so it is a holomorphic $1$-form on $\mathbb{P}^1\setminus B$.

steps.slogan: Identify the derivative of $\Phi$ with the coefficient of $\tau$.
steps.detail: With $P_i(t)=g_i(t)$, the derivative of $\int_{Q_i}^{g_i(t)}\omega$ in $t$ is the coefficient of $g_i^*\omega$. Summing over $i$ gives $\Phi'(t)\,dt=\tau$ locally.

steps.slogan: Extend $\tau$ holomorphically across each branch value.
steps.detail: Near a point of ramification index $e$ take coordinates with $f=z^e$ and $\omega=\sum a_mz^m\,dz$. With $z_j=\zeta^js$, $s^e=t$, the sum over $j$ keeps only $m+1=ke$ and equals $\sum_{k\ge1}(a_{ke-1}/k)\,d(t^k)$. This is holomorphic in $t$, also at $t=\infty$ in the coordinate $1/t$.

steps.slogan: Show that a holomorphic $1$-form on the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere) is zero.
steps.detail: Now $\tau=g(t)\,dt$ with $g$ entire. At $\infty$, with $w=1/t$, the form $-g(1/w)w^{-2}dw$ is holomorphic, so $g(t)=O(|t|^{-2})$. A bounded entire function is constant, and this one tends to $0$, so $g=0$ and $\tau=0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the sum $\Phi$ of integrals is constant.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 4 give $\Phi'=0$ on the connected set $\mathbb{P}^1\setminus B$. So $\Phi$ is constant along every path of $t$ that avoids $B$, and continuity of integrals extends this across $B$. A different choice of paths adds periods of $\omega$.

concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: Compactness gives finite fibres and a finite set of branch values.
concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The moving points are the fibres of a meromorphic function.
concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The surface is the Riemann surface of a smooth projective algebraic curve.
concepts.c:abelian-integral: The sum of abelian integrals over the fibre is the quantity that stays constant.
concepts.c:riemann-sphere: The sphere carries no nonzero holomorphic $1$-form.

source.note: The trace proof of Abel's theorem, as in Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry, Chapter 2.

statement: Let $M$ be a sphere with a metric that is locally Euclidean except at finitely many cone points, each of total angle less than $2\pi$. Then $M$ is isometric, for the [intrinsic metric](c:intrinsic-metric), to the surface of a [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (possibly a doubly covered convex polygon). The polyhedron is unique up to rigid motion and reflection.

hypotheses.text: The metric space $M$ is homeomorphic to the $2$-sphere and is locally Euclidean except at finitely many cone points.
Every cone point has total angle less than $2\pi$, that is, positive curvature.

conclusion: The surface $M$ is isometric to the surface of a [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron), unique up to congruence.

proofs.name: Continuity method on polyhedral metrics
proofs.slogan: Compare the manifold of convex polyhedra with the manifold of polyhedral metrics, show the surface-metric map is injective, open and closed, and conclude that it is onto.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, as an outline of Alexandrov's proof; the compactness and the degenerate cases rest on the cited book. The uniqueness half is the Cauchy-Alexandrov rigidity theorem.

roles.why: The sphere with a flat structure away from cone points is the space that a polyhedral surface realizes.
Positive curvature at each cone point is the condition that a convex cone has, and it makes $\sum(2\pi-\theta_i)=4\pi$.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the metrics by their cone points and triangulations to get a connected manifold $\mathcal{M}_n$.
steps.detail: Cut $M$ into Euclidean triangles with vertices at the $n$ cone points. The edge lengths give charts, and the angle sum condition $\sum_i (2\pi-\theta_i) = 4\pi$ holds by the Gauss-Bonnet formula for such metrics. The set $\mathcal{M}_n$ of such metrics up to isometry is a connected manifold of dimension $3n-6$.

steps.slogan: Prove that convex polyhedra with isometric surfaces are congruent.
steps.detail: This is Alexandrov's extension of Cauchy's rigidity lemma: a sign-change count along the edges of the two polyhedra excludes a nontrivial infinitesimal or finite deformation that keeps the surface metric. So the map $\Phi$ from polyhedra with $n$ labelled vertices to $\mathcal{M}_n$ is injective, which is the uniqueness half.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi$ is open by invariance of domain.
steps.detail: The space of nondegenerate convex polyhedra with $n$ labelled vertices, modulo rigid motions, is a manifold of the same dimension $3n-6$. An injective continuous map between manifolds of equal dimension is open.

steps.slogan: Show that the image of $\Phi$ is closed using compactness of limits of polyhedra.
steps.detail: A sequence of polyhedra with bounded diameter has a convergent subsequence by the Blaschke selection theorem. The limit is a convex surface, possibly degenerate, whose metric is the limit metric. Vertices that merge or a collapse to a doubly covered polygon are handled as separate cases.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\Phi$ is onto, so every polyhedral metric is realized.
steps.detail: The image of $\Phi$ is open and closed in the connected manifold $\mathcal{M}_n$ and is nonempty. So it is all of $\mathcal{M}_n$, and $M$ is the surface of a convex polyhedron, unique by step 2.

concepts.c:intrinsic-metric: The theorem compares the intrinsic metric of a surface with its shape.
concepts.c:convex-polyhedron: The realizing object is a convex polyhedron, possibly doubly covered.

source.ref: A. D. Alexandrov, Convex Polyhedra, Springer Monographs in Mathematics, Springer, Berlin, 2005 (translation of the 1950 Russian edition)
source.note: Alexandrov's gluing theorem and its uniqueness; Bobenko and Izmestiev, Ann. Inst. Fourier 58 (2008), give a variational proof.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over $\mathbb{C}$, with [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor) $K_X$ and topological [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) $e(X)$. Then $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=\dfrac{K_X^2+e(X)}{12}$.

hypotheses.text: The variety $X$ is a smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over $\mathbb{C}$.

proofs.name: Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch
proofs.slogan: Write $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)$ as an integral of the [Todd class](c:todd-class) and read its degree-two part through $c_1^2=K_X^2$ and $c_2=e(X)$.
proofs.scope: Noether's formula, the member of the family that the packet scores. Max Noether's other theorem on plane curves is a different statement and is not proved here.

roles.why: Smoothness and projectivity give a compact complex manifold of dimension $2$ with Chern classes $c_1,c_2$ and a canonical divisor.

steps.slogan: Write $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)$ as an integral over $X$ by the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem.
steps.detail: For the trivial line bundle the theorem gives $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=\int_X \mathrm{ch}(\mathcal{O}_X)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X)$, where $T_X$ is the holomorphic tangent bundle of the compact complex surface $X$.

steps.slogan: Extract the degree-two part of the [Todd class](c:todd-class) of the tangent bundle.
steps.detail: We have $\mathrm{ch}(\mathcal{O}_X)=1$ and $\mathrm{td}(T_X)=1+\tfrac12c_1+\tfrac1{12}(c_1^2+c_2)+\cdots$ with $c_i=c_i(T_X)$ the [Chern classes](c:chern-class). Only the term of real degree $4$ integrates on a surface, so $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=\tfrac1{12}\int_X(c_1^2+c_2)$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\int_X c_1(T_X)^2$ with $K_X^2$.
steps.detail: The canonical bundle is the determinant of the cotangent bundle, so its class is $-c_1(T_X)$. The sign disappears on squaring, so $\int_X c_1^2=K_X^2$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\int_X c_2(T_X)$ with the Euler characteristic $e(X)$.
steps.detail: The top Chern class of the tangent bundle of a compact complex manifold counts, with sign, the zeros of a generic vector field. By the Poincare-Hopf theorem this count is $e(X)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three integrals into $12\,\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=K_X^2+e(X)$.
steps.detail: Substitute steps 3 and 4 into the formula of step 2. This gives $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=\tfrac1{12}(K_X^2+e(X))$.

concepts.c:algebraic-surface: The theorem concerns a smooth projective surface.
concepts.c:canonical-divisor: The square of the canonical divisor is the term $K_X^2$.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The topological Euler characteristic is the integral of $c_2$.
concepts.c:todd-class: The Todd class carries the coefficient $1/12$ in degree two.
concepts.c:chern-class: The classes $c_1$ and $c_2$ turn into $K_X^2$ and $e(X)$.

source.note: Noether's formula from the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem, as in Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Appendix A.

statement: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $A_1,\dots,A_{2n}$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $R$. Then $\sum_{\sigma \in S_{2n}} \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\,A_{\sigma(1)}\cdots A_{\sigma(2n)} = 0$. So the [matrix ring](c:matrix-ring) $M_n(R)$ satisfies a [polynomial identity](c:polynomial-identity) of degree $2n$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with identity.
The elements $A_1,\dots,A_{2n}$ lie in the [matrix ring](c:matrix-ring) $M_n(R)$.

conclusion: The standard polynomial $S_{2n}(A_1,\dots,A_{2n})$ is the zero matrix.

proofs.name: Rosset's Grassmann algebra proof
proofs.slogan: Put the matrices in one matrix over a Grassmann algebra, show that its square has commuting entries and zero traces, and apply Cayley-Hamilton.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$ and all commutative rings $R$. The case of a general $R$ is reduced to a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra in the first step.

roles.why: Commutativity of $R$ makes the even part of the Grassmann algebra commutative, which allows Cayley-Hamilton.
The matrices $A_k$ are the coefficients of the Grassmann combination $X$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to matrices with entries in a commutative $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra.
steps.detail: The entries of $S_{2n}(A_1,\dots,A_{2n})$ are integer polynomials in the entries of the $A_k$. It suffices to prove the identity for generic matrices over $\mathbb{Z}[x^{(k)}_{ij}]$, a subring of $\mathbb{Q}[x^{(k)}_{ij}]$, since every $R$ is reached by a ring homomorphism. So we assume that $2$ is invertible in $R$.

steps.slogan: Form the matrix $X=\sum_k e_kA_k$ over the Grassmann algebra on $e_1,\dots,e_{2n}$.
steps.detail: Let $E$ be the exterior algebra over $R$ on $e_1,\dots,e_{2n}$, and $X=\sum_{k=1}^{2n}e_kA_k \in M_n(E)$. Since $e_{\sigma(1)}\cdots e_{\sigma(2n)}=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)e_1\cdots e_{2n}$, the coefficient of $e_1\cdots e_{2n}$ in $X^{2n}$ is $S_{2n}(A_1,\dots,A_{2n})$. So it suffices to show $X^{2n}=0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the entries of $Y=X^2$ lie in the commutative even part $E_0$.
steps.detail: Each entry of $Y$ is a sum of products $e_ke_l$ times elements of $R$, so it lies in the even part $E_0$ of $E$. The ring $E_0$ is commutative because $R$ is and even elements commute with all elements.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{tr}(Y^j)=0$ for all $j\ge1$.
steps.detail: The entries of $X^{2j-1}$ are odd and odd elements anticommute, so $\mathrm{tr}(X\cdot X^{2j-1})=-\mathrm{tr}(X^{2j-1}\cdot X)$. Thus $2\,\mathrm{tr}(X^{2j})=0$, and $\mathrm{tr}(Y^j)=\mathrm{tr}(X^{2j})=0$ because $2$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Apply the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to $Y$ over $E_0$ to get $Y^n=0$ and so $S_{2n}=0$.
steps.detail: Over the commutative $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra $E_0$, the matrix $Y$ satisfies its characteristic polynomial. By Newton's identities the coefficients are rational polynomials in the traces $\mathrm{tr}(Y^j)$ with no constant term, so they vanish. Thus $X^{2n}=Y^n=0$, and the coefficient $S_{2n}$ of $e_1\cdots e_{2n}$ is zero.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity of the even part allows the characteristic polynomial argument.
concepts.c:matrix-ring: The identity holds on the matrix ring $M_n(R)$.
concepts.c:polynomial-identity: The theorem says that $S_{2n}$ is a polynomial identity of $M_n(R)$.

source.note: S. Rosset, A new proof of the Amitsur-Levitski identity, Israel Journal of Mathematics 23 (1976), 187-188.

statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a symmetric [convex body](c:convex-body) and $f \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to [0,\infty)$ an integrable, symmetric, [unimodal function](c:unimodal-function), so every set $\{f \ge c\}$ is convex. Then $\int_{K+ty} f\,dx \ge \int_{K+y} f\,dx$ for every $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $0 \le t \le 1$.

hypotheses.text: The set $K$ is a [convex body](c:convex-body) with $K=-K$.
The function $f \ge 0$ is integrable, satisfies $f(-x)=f(x)$, and every set $\{f \ge c\}$ is convex.

conclusion: Moving $K$ toward the origin does not decrease the integral of $f$ over it.

proofs.name: Brunn-Minkowski and level sets
proofs.slogan: Cut $f$ into symmetric convex level sets, and show that the volume of the section through a translate is an even function with a concave $n$-th root.
proofs.scope: All $y$ and $t \in [0,1]$. If the volume at $s=1$ is zero, the inequality is trivial, and the steps assume that it is positive.

roles.why: Convexity of $K$ makes the lifted set convex, and $K=-K$ makes the section volume even.
Unimodality gives convex level sets, symmetry makes them symmetric, and integrability allows Fubini.

steps.slogan: Write $f$ as an integral over its level sets and reduce to one symmetric convex set $L$.
steps.detail: With $L_c=\{f\ge c\}$ we have $\int_A f=\int_0^\infty\mathrm{vol}(A\cap L_c)\,dc$ for measurable $A$, by Fubini. Each $L_c$ is [convex](c:convex-set) and symmetric, so it suffices to show $g(t)\ge g(1)$ for $g(s)=\mathrm{vol}(L\cap(K+sy))$.

steps.slogan: Lift to the convex set $C=\{(x,s):x\in L,\ x-sy\in K\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
steps.detail: The set $C$ is the intersection of two preimages of convex sets under linear maps, so it is convex. Its section at height $s$ is $L\cap(K+sy)$, of volume $g(s)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $g^{1/n}$ is concave on the interval where $g>0$.
steps.detail: For $0<\lambda<1$, the section of $C$ at $(1-\lambda)s_0+\lambda s_1$ contains $(1-\lambda)C_{s_0}+\lambda C_{s_1}$. The Brunn-Minkowski inequality gives $g((1-\lambda)s_0+\lambda s_1)^{1/n}\ge(1-\lambda)g(s_0)^{1/n}+\lambda g(s_1)^{1/n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ is even, using the symmetry of $K$ and of $L$.
steps.detail: The map $x\mapsto -x$ sends $L\cap(K+sy)$ onto $(-L)\cap(-K-sy)$, which equals $L\cap(K-sy)$ because $L=-L$ and $K=-K$. The map preserves volume, so $g(-s)=g(s)$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $g$ does not increase on $[0,\infty)$ and integrate over the levels $c$.
steps.detail: If $g(1)=0$ there is nothing to show. Otherwise let $h=g^{1/n}$, which is even and concave by steps 3 and 4. Then $h(0)\ge\tfrac12(h(-1)+h(1))=h(1)$, and concavity on $[0,1]$ gives $h(t)\ge(1-t)h(0)+th(1)\ge h(1)$. So $g(t)\ge g(1)$ for every level, and integration over $c$ gives the theorem.

concepts.c:convex-body: A symmetric convex body $K$ is the set that is translated.
concepts.c:unimodal-function: Convex level sets let the Brunn-Minkowski inequality apply.
concepts.c:convex-set: The level sets and the lifted set are convex, which gives concavity.

source.note: The Brunn-Minkowski proof of Anderson's theorem, as in Gardner, The Brunn-Minkowski inequality, Bulletin of the AMS 39 (2002).

statement: Let $g(z)=z+b_0+b_1z^{-1}+b_2z^{-2}+\cdots$ be [univalent](c:univalent-function), that is holomorphic and injective, on $\{|z|>1\}$. Then $\sum_{n\ge1}n|b_n|^2\le1$.

hypotheses.text: The function $g$ is [univalent](c:univalent-function) on $\{|z|>1\}$.
On $\{|z|>1\}$ the function has the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) $g(z)=z+b_0+\sum_{n\ge1}b_nz^{-n}$.

proofs.name: Area of the image of a circle
proofs.slogan: Compute the area enclosed by the image of the circle $|z|=r$ with Green's theorem, and use that it is not negative.
proofs.scope: The whole inequality, with the series possibly infinite. The area is computed for each $r>1$, and the limit $r\to1^+$ is taken at the end.

roles.why: Injectivity makes the image of each circle a Jordan curve that bounds a region of area at least zero.
The Laurent series gives $\bar g$ and $g'$ explicitly, so that the area integral is computable term by term.

steps.slogan: Take the Jordan curve $\Gamma_r=g(\{|z|=r\})$ for $r>1$ and the region $D_r$ that it bounds.
steps.detail: Injectivity of $g$ makes $\Gamma_r$ a simple closed curve, so it bounds a region $D_r$ of area $A_r\ge0$ by the Jordan curve theorem. Since $g(z)\sim z$ near infinity, the argument principle shows that $\Gamma_r$ runs once counterclockwise.

steps.slogan: Write the area $A_r$ as a contour integral by Green's theorem.
steps.detail: For the positively oriented boundary of $D_r$, Green's theorem gives $A_r=\frac1{2i}\oint_{\Gamma_r}\bar w\,dw$. Substituting $w=g(z)$ along the circle gives $A_r=\frac1{2i}\oint_{|z|=r}\overline{g(z)}\,g'(z)\,dz$.

steps.slogan: Insert the Laurent series and integrate term by term over $z=re^{i\theta}$.
steps.detail: With $dz=iz\,d\theta$ we get $A_r=\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}\bar g\,(z-\sum nb_nz^{-n})\,d\theta$. Orthogonality of $e^{ik\theta}$ keeps only $r^2$ from $\bar g z$ and $nb_n\bar b_nr^{-2n}$ from the sum. So $A_r=\pi\bigl(r^2-\sum_{n\ge1}n|b_n|^2r^{-2n}\bigr)$.

steps.slogan: Use $A_r\ge0$ for every $r>1$ and let $r\to1^+$ to bound the series.
steps.detail: For each $N$ and $r>1$, $\sum_{n=1}^Nn|b_n|^2r^{-2n}\le r^2$ because the terms are not negative. Let $r\to1^+$ to get $\sum_{n=1}^Nn|b_n|^2\le1$, and then let $N\to\infty$.

concepts.c:univalent-function: Injectivity makes the image of each circle a simple closed curve.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The coefficients $b_n$ of the Laurent series appear in the area formula.

source.note: Gronwall's area theorem; the proof is the one in Duren, Univalent Functions, Section 2.1.

statement: Let two agents share a [prior](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on a finite set $\Omega$ with $\mu(\{\omega\})>0$ and hold information partitions $\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_2$. For an event $E$, let $q_i(\omega)=\mu(E\mid\mathcal{P}_i(\omega))$. If at a state $\omega^*$ it is [common knowledge](c:common-knowledge) that $q_1=\eta_1$ and $q_2=\eta_2$, then $\eta_1=\eta_2$.

hypotheses.text: Both agents use one [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on a finite set $\Omega$ with $\mu(\{\omega\})>0$ for all $\omega$.
Agent $i$ is informed by a partition $\mathcal{P}_i$ of $\Omega$ and holds the [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) $q_i(\omega)=\mu(E\mid\mathcal{P}_i(\omega))$.
At the state $\omega^*$ it is [common knowledge](c:common-knowledge) that $q_1=\eta_1$ and $q_2=\eta_2$.

conclusion: The two posterior probabilities are equal: $\eta_1=\eta_2$.

proofs.name: Meet of the partitions
proofs.slogan: Restrict to the cell of the meet of the two partitions that holds $\omega^*$, and compute $\mu(E\cap M)$ in two ways.
proofs.scope: A finite state space. The same proof works for a countable space with positive prior mass.

roles.why: The common prior makes both computations of $\mu(E\cap M)$ use the same measure, and positive mass gives $\mu(M)>0$.
The cells of $\mathcal{P}_i$ give the posteriors and tile $M$.
Common knowledge says that the two posterior values are constant on $M$.

steps.slogan: Take the cell $M$ of the finest common coarsening of $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ that holds $\omega^*$.
steps.detail: This cell $M$ is the set of states reached from $\omega^*$ by alternating steps inside cells of $\mathcal{P}_1$ and of $\mathcal{P}_2$. An event is [common knowledge](c:common-knowledge) at $\omega^*$ exactly when it contains $M$. Also $M$ is a union of cells of $\mathcal{P}_1$ and a union of cells of $\mathcal{P}_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $q_1=\eta_1$ and $q_2=\eta_2$ at every state of $M$.
steps.detail: The event $\{q_1=\eta_1\}\cap\{q_2=\eta_2\}$ is common knowledge at $\omega^*$, so it contains $M$. Hence $q_1\equiv\eta_1$ and $q_2\equiv\eta_2$ on $M$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the cells of $\mathcal{P}_1$ inside $M$ to get $\mu(E\cap M)=\eta_1\mu(M)$.
steps.detail: Write $M=\bigsqcup_kC_k$ with $C_k\in\mathcal{P}_1$. On each cell $\mu(E\cap C_k)=q_1\mu(C_k)=\eta_1\mu(C_k)$, and adding over $k$ gives $\mu(E\cap M)=\eta_1\mu(M)$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the sum over the cells of $\mathcal{P}_2$ to get $\mu(E\cap M)=\eta_2\mu(M)$.
steps.detail: The cell $M$ is also a disjoint union of cells of $\mathcal{P}_2$, on each of which $q_2=\eta_2$. The same computation gives $\mu(E\cap M)=\eta_2\mu(M)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\mu(M)>0$ to get $\eta_1=\eta_2$.
steps.detail: The set $M$ is nonempty and every state has positive mass, so $\mu(M)>0$. Comparing the two expressions for $\mu(E\cap M)$ gives $\eta_1\mu(M)=\eta_2\mu(M)$, so $\eta_1=\eta_2$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: The shared prior is one probability measure used by both agents.
concepts.c:common-knowledge: Common knowledge makes both posteriors constant on the meet cell.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: The posteriors are conditional probabilities of $E$ on the information cells.

source.note: R. J. Aumann, Agreeing to disagree, Annals of Statistics 4 (1976), 1236-1239.

statement: Let $P$ be a convex polytope of dimension $d$. Its graph, formed by the vertices and edges of $P$, has more than $d$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any $d-1$ vertices. That is, the graph has [connectivity](c:graph-connectivity) at least $d$.

hypotheses.text: The set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is a [convex polytope](c:convex-polytope) of dimension $d$.

conclusion: The graph of $P$ has more than $d$ vertices, and removing any set of at most $d-1$ vertices leaves a connected graph.

proofs.name: Hyperplane through the removed vertices
proofs.slogan: Cut by a hyperplane through the removed vertices, climb edge paths to the extreme faces, and join the two sides through a vertex on the hyperplane.
proofs.scope: All $d\ge1$ and every vertex set $S$ with $|S|\le d-1$. The graph of a face is connected, which follows from the climbing step with a generic functional.

roles.why: Full dimension gives at least $d+1$ vertices, edges generating each vertex cone, and points on both sides of a hyperplane.

steps.slogan: Choose a hyperplane $H=\{f=0\}$ through the removed vertices and one more vertex.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be a set of at most $d-1$ vertices. A $d$-dimensional polytope has at least $d+1$ vertices, so there is a vertex $v_0\notin S$. The at most $d$ points of $S\cup\{v_0\}$ lie in a hyperplane $H$, the zero set of an affine function $f$. Since $P$ has dimension $d$, $P\not\subset H$.

steps.slogan: Climb along edges from any vertex to a vertex where $f$ is maximal.
steps.detail: The edge directions at a vertex $v$ generate the cone of directions into $P$. If $f(v)<\max_P f$, this cone holds a direction with $f$ increasing, so some edge at $v$ strictly increases $f$. Repeating gives an edge path along which $f$ strictly increases, and it ends on the face $F^+$ where $f$ is maximal. The same works downward to the face $F^-$ where $f$ is minimal.

steps.slogan: Join every vertex off $H$ to the top or the bottom face without touching $S$.
steps.detail: A vertex with $f>0$ climbs through vertices with $f>0$ to $F^+$, so the path avoids $S\subset H$. A vertex with $f<0$ descends to $F^-$ in the same way. The graph of a [convex polytope](c:convex-polytope) face is connected, since a generic functional climbs from every vertex to its single maximum, so each side is connected.

steps.slogan: Join every vertex on $H$ outside $S$ to the vertices off $H$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be a vertex on $H$ with $v\notin S$. Because $P\not\subset H$, the cone at $v$ holds a direction with $f>0$ or with $f<0$, so $v$ has a neighbor off $H$. If $P$ has points on both sides of $H$, then $v$ has neighbors on both sides, so $v_0$ joins the two sides.

steps.slogan: Combine the pieces to show that the graph minus $S$ is connected.
steps.detail: The vertices with $f>0$ form one component with $F^+$, and those with $f<0$ form one with $F^-$. Every vertex on $H$ outside $S$ is adjacent to one of them, and $v_0$ links the two components when both exist. So the graph minus $S$ is connected for every $S$ with $|S|\le d-1$, and the graph has more than $d$ vertices.

concepts.c:graph-connectivity: The theorem gives a lower bound $d$ for the connectivity of the graph.
concepts.c:convex-polytope: The polytope supplies the vertices, edges and faces that the climbing uses.

source.note: M. L. Balinski, On the graph structure of convex polyhedra in n-space, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 11 (1961), 431-434; see Ziegler, Lectures on Polytopes, Theorem 3.14.

statement: Take a [renormalizable](c:renormalizable-interaction) local interaction, for example $\varphi^4$ in four dimensions. For every [Feynman diagram](c:feynman-diagram), Bogoliubov's R-operation subtracts counterterms that are polynomial in momenta and masses, and the subtracted amplitude is finite. So the [renormalized](c:renormalization) Green's functions and S-matrix elements have no ultraviolet divergences at any order of perturbation theory.

hypotheses.text: The interaction is a [renormalizable](c:renormalizable-interaction) local polynomial interaction, for example $\varphi^4$ in four dimensions.
The object $\Gamma$ is a [Feynman diagram](c:feynman-diagram) of the theory, of any fixed order.

conclusion: The R-operation gives a finite amplitude for every diagram, with local counterterms, so renormalized Green's functions and S-matrix elements are free of ultraviolet divergences at every order.

proofs.name: Forest formula and Hepp sectors
proofs.slogan: Count the divergence of every subdiagram, subtract Taylor polynomials by the forest formula, and bound the subtracted integrand sector by sector.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof of Hepp and Zimmermann for massive scalar theory with Euclidean propagators; the sector estimates rest on the cited paper. Other renormalizable interactions follow the same scheme.

roles.why: Renormalizability bounds the divergence degree of a subdiagram by its external lines alone, so only polynomial counterterms appear.
Each diagram has finitely many subdiagrams, so the recursion and the forest sum are finite.

steps.slogan: Count the superficial degree of divergence $\omega(\gamma)$ of every subdiagram $\gamma$.
steps.detail: For $\varphi^4$ in four dimensions $\omega(\gamma)=4-E(\gamma)$, with $E(\gamma)$ the number of external lines. The degree depends only on the external lines because the interaction is [renormalizable](c:renormalizable-interaction). A subdiagram diverges when $\omega(\gamma)\ge0$.

steps.slogan: Define the R-operation recursively by Taylor subtraction at each divergent subdiagram.
steps.detail: Bogoliubov's recursion subtracts from each divergent subdiagram $\gamma$ the Taylor polynomial of degree $\omega(\gamma)$ in its external momenta, working from the smallest subdiagrams upward. This gives $R_\Gamma$ by induction on the size of $\Gamma$.

steps.slogan: Solve the recursion by Zimmermann's forest formula.
steps.detail: The recursion is solved by a sum over forests, which are families of nested or disjoint divergent subdiagrams, of products of Taylor subtraction operators. This gives $R_\Gamma$ as an explicit integrand.

steps.slogan: Split the loop-momentum space into Hepp sectors and bound the integrand in each sector.
steps.detail: Hepp orders the loop momenta by scale, which gives finitely many sectors. In each sector Weinberg's power counting, with the subtractions of step 3, gives an integrable decay of $R_\Gamma$. So the amplitude converges absolutely.

steps.slogan: Observe that the counterterms are local, so the finite amplitudes are the renormalized ones.
steps.detail: The subtracted Taylor polynomials are polynomials in momenta and masses of degree at most $\omega(\gamma)$. They are local counterterms that shift the parameters of the Lagrangian, so [renormalization](c:renormalization) gives finite Green's functions and S-matrix elements at every order.

concepts.c:renormalizable-interaction: Renormalizability limits the divergence degree to the external lines.
concepts.c:feynman-diagram: The theorem is a statement about every Feynman diagram.
concepts.c:renormalization: Subtracting local counterterms is the renormalization that gives finite results.

source.ref: K. Hepp, Proof of the Bogoliubov-Parasiuk theorem on renormalization, Communications in Mathematical Physics 2 (1966), 301-326
source.note: After N. N. Bogoliubov and O. S. Parasiuk, Acta Math. 97 (1957); Zimmermann's forest formula is in Comm. Math. Phys. 15 (1969).

statement: If a [hexagon](c:hexagon) $A_1A_2\cdots A_6$ is circumscribed about a [conic section](c:conic-section), that is, its six sides are tangent to the conic, then its three main diagonals $A_1A_4$, $A_2A_5$ and $A_3A_6$ meet in one point.

hypotheses.text: The curve $C$ is a nondegenerate [conic section](c:conic-section) in the [projective plane](c:projective-plane).
The six sides of the hexagon are distinct tangent lines of $C$, and $A_i$ is the meeting point of side $s_i$ and side $s_{i+1}$.

conclusion: The lines $A_1A_4$, $A_2A_5$ and $A_3A_6$ pass through one point.

proofs.name: Polarity and Pascal's theorem
proofs.slogan: Take the polar of each vertex with respect to the conic to get an inscribed hexagon, apply Pascal's theorem, and take the pole of the Pascal line.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem in the projective plane, so that parallel lines and points at infinity need no separate case. Brianchon's theorem is the dual of Pascal's theorem, and this proof uses that duality.

roles.why: The conic defines the polarity that swaps points and lines, and the tangent at a point of $C$ is its polar.
Six distinct tangents give six distinct touching points $T_i$ that form an inscribed hexagon.

steps.slogan: Name the touching point $T_i$ of each side $s_i$ with the conic.
steps.detail: Let $s_i$ touch the conic at $T_i$, and let $A_i=s_i\cap s_{i+1}$ with indices modulo $6$. The six points $T_i$ are distinct because the six tangents are distinct, so $T_1\cdots T_6$ is a hexagon inscribed in the conic.

steps.slogan: Show that the [polar](c:pole-and-polar) of the vertex $A_i$ is the chord $T_iT_{i+1}$.
steps.detail: The point $A_i$ lies on the tangents at $T_i$ and at $T_{i+1}$. By La Hire's theorem, $T_i$ and $T_{i+1}$ lie on the polar of $A_i$. So this polar is the line $T_iT_{i+1}$.

steps.slogan: Apply Pascal's theorem to the inscribed hexagon $T_1\cdots T_6$.
steps.detail: Let $P_1=T_1T_2\cap T_4T_5$, $P_2=T_2T_3\cap T_5T_6$ and $P_3=T_3T_4\cap T_6T_1$ be the meeting points of opposite sides. Pascal's theorem says that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ lie on one line $\ell$.

steps.slogan: Show that the polar of $P_j$ is the diagonal $A_jA_{j+3}$.
steps.detail: The point $P_1$ lies on the polars $T_1T_2$ of $A_1$ and $T_4T_5$ of $A_4$. By La Hire's theorem, $A_1$ and $A_4$ lie on the polar of $P_1$. The points $A_1\ne A_4$ because no point lies on four tangents of a conic, so that polar is the line $A_1A_4$. The same holds for $j=2,3$.

steps.slogan: Dualize the collinearity of $P_1,P_2,P_3$ to the concurrence of the diagonals.
steps.detail: The points $P_1,P_2,P_3$ lie on $\ell$. By La Hire's theorem, their polars, which are the three main diagonals, all pass through the pole $Q$ of $\ell$.

concepts.c:hexagon: The circumscribed hexagon and its inscribed partner are the objects.
concepts.c:conic-section: The conic defines the polarity and carries the tangency points.
concepts.c:projective-plane: The projective plane makes every two lines meet, with no exceptions.
concepts.c:pole-and-polar: Poles and polars turn vertices into chords and collinear points into concurrent lines.

source.note: The classical duality proof through Pascal's theorem; see Coxeter, Projective Geometry.
